title: Compounds and Reactions with Oxygen
seo_title: Grade 9 Natural Sciences: Compounds and Reactions with Oxygen Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 9 Natural Sciences: Compounds; chemical reactions; reactions of metals and non-metals with oxygen
standard_text: Compounds are formed when atoms of different elements combine; chemical formulas and names. Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides (rusting, burning); non-metals react with oxygen to form non-metal oxides; balanced equations. (summary of CAPS Natural Sciences, Grade 9, Matter and Materials: Compounds; chemical reactions; reactions of metals and non-metals with oxygen)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Natural Sciences worksheets (CAPS): elements and compounds, names and formulas, metals and non-metals reacting with oxygen, and balanced equations. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

A compound has atoms of two or more elements chemically joined, in fixed amounts: water (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), sodium chloride (NaCl). Compound names often end in -ide when two elements are joined.

Metals react with oxygen to make metal oxides: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (bright white flame); iron rusts slowly to form iron oxide. Non-metals burn in oxygen to make non-metal oxides: C + O2 → CO2; S + O2 → SO2. Sulfur dioxide from burning coal causes acid rain.

Example

Name the product of magnesium burning in oxygen.

Metal + oxygen

Answer: magnesium oxide

Example

How many atoms are in one molecule of CO2?

1 C + 2 O

Answer: 3

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a compound is a mixture.
  • Reading CO as cobalt.
  • Thinking rusting needs only water.

faq.q: Why does burning coal cause acid rain?
faq.a: Coal contains sulfur, which forms sulfur dioxide that dissolves in rain.

faq.q: Are metal oxides acidic or basic?
faq.a: Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.

items.q: Which coefficients (in order) balance this equation? C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
items.e: Check: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? ?H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>
items.e: Balanced: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: What number replaces ? to balance the equation? C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + ?H<sub>2</sub>O
items.e: Balanced: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
c: No. There are more molecules on the right.
Yes. Each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.
items.e: Count each element on both sides.

items.q: Is this equation balanced? N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 4NH<sub>3</sub>
c: No. H has 6 atoms on the left and 12 on the right.
No. There are too many arrows.
Yes. Both sides have the same elements.
